summary:
ORBITCRAFT: An Interactive Space Mission Design Game. It is a simulation for individuals or teams of up to four to design, manage, and evaluate space missions. It addresses a learning gap: students study orbital mechanics, spacecraft systems, launch vehicles, and communications separately without experiencing how these elements interact in a mission. 
Players define objectives, configure spacecraft and instruments, choose an orbit and launch vehicle, and manage six resources: mass, power, budget, data, communications, and time. Instrument choices may improve scientific value while increasing mass, power demand, data generation, and cost. Dashboards, mission validation, simulation, and post-mission reports make these trade-offs understandable. 
The simulation connects to NASA systems engineering, the four mission segments—launch, space, ground, and user—and the lifecycle from concept development through operations and closeout. Concept Maturity Levels provide a framework for progressing from an initial idea to a point design. Resources include NASA’s Mission Design Lab, GMAT, NASA Mission Viz, CubeSat 101, Microsoft Planetary Computer, Orekit, and Basilisk. 
This is a modular game, beginning with a core simulator and adding analysis, visualization, and collaboration. Engineering outputs use available parameters, distinguishing simplified models from validated analyses, and explicitly identifying missing data rather than invented results.
details:
This project developed the concept for an Interactive Space Mission Design Game, an educational simulation that helps students and aspiring engineers understand the complexities of real-world space mission development. It addresses the gap between theoretical learning and practical experience by allowing individuals or teams of up to four participants to design, manage, and simulate complete space missions.

Users define mission objectives, configure spacecraft, select scientific instruments, choose launch vehicles and orbits, and manage essential resources, including mass, power, budget, data, communications, and mission lifetime. The simulation demonstrates how engineering decisions create interconnected trade-offs and influence mission success. Its creative approach combines interactive visualizations, collaborative decision-making, resource management, and mission-performance evaluation in one learning environment.

The data draws on NASA's systems-engineering guidelines, JPL's Concept Maturity Levels, NASA's Mission Design Lab, GMAT, NASA Mission Viz, CubeSat 101, and Microsoft Planetary Computer. Key considerations include engineering feasibility, scientific objectives, resource limitations, orbital constraints, communications, cost, and operational lifetime.

Our ORBITCRAFT aims to make space engineering more accessible, encourage critical thinking and teamwork, strengthen practical engineering knowledge, and inspire the next generation of space scientists and engineers.
